title: Buffer Overflow Attacks and Defenses

sections.heading: Stack Frames and the Anatomy of an Overflow
sections.body:
A function call in the x86-64 System V ABI leaves a stack frame that mixes two kinds of data with no hardware separation between them: the callee's local variables and the control information the CPU needs to resume the caller. When `P` calls `Q`, `Q`'s frame holds (from high to low addresses, since the x86-64 stack grows downward) the return address pushed by `call`, then any saved registers `Q` must restore, then `Q`'s own local variables. A local array such as `char buf[64]` is just a contiguous block of bytes at a fixed offset from `%rsp`; C performs no bounds checking on array writes, so a function that copies attacker-controlled input into `buf` with an unchecked routine such as `gets` writes exactly as many bytes as the input string contains, regardless of `buf`'s declared size.

Because the return address sits at a higher address than the buffer, in the same frame, an input long enough to fill `buf` and keep going overwrites the return address with attacker-chosen bytes. When `Q` executes `ret`, the CPU pops whatever eight bytes now occupy that slot into `%rip` and jumps there unconditionally — the processor has no way to tell a legitimate return address from one supplied by the attacker's own input. This is the invariant every defense in this card is built to break: on an unprotected stack, control data (the return address) and program data (the buffer's contents) occupy the same trusted memory region, so any unchecked write into the data can become a write into the control path.

sections.heading: Code Injection: Building an Exploit String
sections.body:
A code-injection attack packs three things into one input string: the byte encoding of executable machine instructions ("shellcode"), padding bytes to occupy the space between the start of the buffer and the return-address slot, and a pointer value — placed exactly where the return address lives — that points back into the buffer itself. When the vulnerable function returns, `ret` jumps into the attacker's injected bytes instead of resuming the caller. CS:APP's Attack Lab (`CTARGET`) drills exactly this construction: phases 1–3 (worth 10, 25 and 25 of the 50 points needed to pass) each redirect execution to a different target function — `touch1`, `touch2`, `touch3` — through exploit strings of increasing sophistication, all built against the same vulnerable entry point, `getbuf`, whose entire job is `Gets(buf)` into a small stack buffer.

Two properties make `CTARGET` exploitable at all: the program is built so stack addresses stay consistent from run to run, and the stack is marked executable, so bytes written there can also be fetched as instructions. The lab's rules make the construction concrete without letting an exploit cheat the validation logic around it: any address used by a `ret` must resolve to `touch1`, `touch2` or `touch3`, to the attacker's own injected code, or — in the ROP phase — to a gadget inside the target's designated gadget farm, never to an address that merely happens to skip a check. That constraint is what turns the exercise from "crash the program any way you can" into "demonstrate the exact overwrite-the-return-address primitive the course is teaching."

sections.heading: Defenses: Canaries, ASLR, and NX/DEP
sections.body:
Three independent defenses attack the code-injection primitive from different angles, and METU's own midterm treats them as the three correct answers to "what stops this attack" (with "digitally signing the executable on disk" offered as a deliberately wrong option, since it protects against tampering with the binary at rest, not against a runtime write into the stack).

**Stack canaries.** The compiler inserts a random word between the local buffer and the saved registers/return address, plus a check before every `ret`:

```text
movq 8(%rsp), %rax    # retrieve the canary from the stack
xorq %fs:40, %rax     # compare it to the reference value
je   .L6               # unchanged -> fall through to a normal return
call __stack_chk_fail  # changed   -> abort instead of returning
```

Because a sequential overflow must overwrite the canary before it can reach the return address above it, corrupting the canary is detected before the corrupted return address is ever used. This is a purely sequential-overwrite defense: it catches nothing if the attacker corrupts some other piece of control data — a function pointer, a saved frame pointer used before the check runs — without touching the canary word itself.

**ASLR (address-space layout randomization).** The kernel places the stack — and, with a position-independent executable, the code and heap too — at a random base address on every run. Code injection depends on the payload containing a pointer to itself; if that address changes every run, a payload built for one run almost never works on the next. ASLR adds no meaningful runtime cost, since the randomization happens once at process start, but it protects nothing once the base address leaks through some other channel: an uninitialized read, a format-string bug, or plain brute-forced guessing when the address space is small.

**NX / DEP (non-executable stack).** The page tables mark the pages backing the stack as not executable, so the CPU raises a fault the instant it tries to fetch an instruction from that region, enforced by hardware on every fetch at the cost of one bit per page-table entry. NX defeats code injection completely regardless of whether the attacker can predict the stack address, because there is nowhere valid to jump the injected bytes to. It does nothing, however, against an attack that never fetches from the stack at all — exactly the gap return-oriented programming is built to exploit.

sections.heading: Return-Oriented Programming: Chaining Existing Code
sections.body:
`RTARGET`, the Attack Lab's second target, combines ASLR (so the stack address is unpredictable) with a non-executable stack (so injected bytes can never run), which together close off code injection entirely. Return-oriented programming answers both defenses at once by never injecting anything: it reuses byte sequences that are already present, already executable, and already mapped inside the program's own code segment.

A **gadget** is any short run of instruction bytes ending in `ret`, encoded as the single byte `0xc3`. The attacker overwrites the stack, starting at the return-address slot, with a sequence of gadget addresses instead of shellcode. When the vulnerable function returns, `ret` jumps to the first gadget; that gadget's own trailing `ret` then pops the next stack slot — the second gadget's address — and jumps there, and so on. The stack itself drives control flow, one `ret` at a time, with no injected code ever touched by the instruction fetcher.

Because x86-64 is a byte-oriented, variable-length instruction set, gadgets don't have to be tail ends of functions the compiler meant to expose. A gadget can be found by jumping into the middle of a compiled function's byte sequence and reinterpreting the following bytes as different instructions than the compiler emitted. The lecture slides' illustration is `ab_plus_c`, compiled (in that example) to `imul %rsi,%rdi`, `lea (%rdi,%rdx,1),%rax`, `ret`; jumping in four bytes early, at the `lea`, yields the shorter gadget `rax <- rdi + rdx; ret` — a sequence the compiler never wrote on purpose. The companion example, a function that stores a fixed constant through a pointer, compiles to a `movl` whose encoded immediate bytes happen to contain a valid `movq %rax, %rdi; ret` a few bytes into the instruction. `RTARGET`'s own rules confine legal gadgets to a designated "gadget farm" region between two marker functions, so the lab has a bounded, deliberately seeded set of these accidental sequences to search rather than the whole binary.

sections.heading: Beyond the Lab: Real Mitigations and Their Trade-offs
sections.body:
Production systems layer more defenses on top of the three above, each closing a specific gap rather than replacing what came before.

**PIE (position-independent executables)** extends ASLR to the code segment itself, not just the stack and heap; without it, ROP against a non-PIE binary can rely on fixed, predictable gadget addresses even while the stack is randomized, since the code segment loads at the same address every run. **RELRO** (relocation read-only) marks the GOT read-only once dynamic linking finishes, closing off a common ROP target used to redirect an indirect call. **Control-flow integrity (CFI)** and hardware **shadow stacks** (Intel CET; pointer authentication on Apple Silicon's arm64e) attack the problem at its root instead of hardening one primitive at a time: CFI restricts every indirect branch to a statically approved set of targets, and a shadow stack keeps a hardware-protected second copy of return addresses that `ret` is checked against, so even a fully successful stack overwrite cannot redirect control flow.

Compilers also don't protect every function equally. GCC's `-fstack-protector`, the common default, only inserts a canary in functions its heuristic flags as containing a vulnerable local — typically an array of at least 8 bytes — while `-fstack-protector-strong` widens that heuristic considerably and `-fstack-protector-all` instruments every function, at a real per-call cost in cycles and code size that grows with how aggressively it is applied. None of this generalizes to the heap: a heap buffer overflow corrupts allocator metadata or adjacent heap objects rather than a return address, so canaries and NX apply differently there, and heap exploitation follows its own separate playbook.

complexity.time: 1 extra load + xor + branch per return
complexity.notes: Checked only at return; corruption that never reaches the canary is undetected

complexity.time: one-time cost at process start, none after
complexity.notes: Any single address leak collapses it to one guess

complexity.time: hardware check on every instruction fetch, free on the legitimate path
complexity.notes: Stops code injection outright; irrelevant to ROP, which never fetches from the stack

complexity.time: one attempt suffices if the stack layout is deterministic
complexity.space: payload ≤ buffer size + padding to the return-address slot
complexity.notes: Defeated by ASLR and NX together

complexity.time: one attempt per gadget chain if code addresses are static
complexity.space: one stack slot per gadget in the chain
complexity.notes: Defeated by PIE (code-segment ASLR) or CFI/shadow stacks

code.caption: A canary-protected frame reproduced with a raw memcpy overflow (no bounds check against buf's 8 bytes). Verified: a 6-byte copy leaves the canary intact; a 16-byte copy overwrites it entirely and the check fires.

worked_example.problem:
A vulnerable frame is laid out exactly as in the code listing:

```c
struct frame { char buf[8]; uint64_t canary; };
```

with `canary` initialized to `0xDEADBEEFCAFEBABE`, and an attacker-controlled `memcpy(f.buf, input, n)` that performs no bounds check against `sizeof(f.buf)`.

(a) With `input = "short"`, `n = 6`, does the post-copy canary check pass?
(b) With `input = "AAAAAAAABBBBBBBB"`, `n = 16`, what does the canary become, and why?
(c) If instead the attacker writes the eight ASCII digit bytes `'0'`,`'1'`,...,`'7'` into the canary's eight bytes, in address order, what 64-bit value does the check compare against, given x86-64's little-endian byte order?
worked_example.solution:
**(a)** `n = 6` writes `"short\0"` into `buf[0..5]`; `buf` is 8 bytes long and `canary` starts at offset 8 (confirmed with `offsetof` on this build: `sizeof(buf) = 8`, `offsetof(canary) = 8`), so the copy never reaches the canary. Running the listing confirms it: `6-byte copy into buf[8]: canary OK, safe return`.

**(b)** `n = 16` writes 16 bytes starting at `buf[0]`. The first 8 bytes (`"AAAAAAAA"`, all `0x41`) exactly fill `buf[0..7]`; the next 8 bytes (`"BBBBBBBB"`, all `0x42`) land precisely on `canary`'s 8 bytes, since `offsetof(canary) == sizeof(buf) == 8`. Every one of those 8 bytes is `0x42`, so regardless of byte order the resulting 64-bit value is
$$\text{canary} = \mathtt{0x4242424242424242}$$
which is exactly what the program prints: `*** stack smashing detected: canary now 4242424242424242 ***`, followed by `16-byte copy into buf[8]: SMASHED`. The check fails because `0x4242424242424242 \neq 0xDEADBEEFCAFEBABE`.

**(c)** Now the 8 bytes written into `canary`, in increasing address order, are `'0','1',...,'7'` i.e. `0x30, 0x31, 0x32, 0x33, 0x34, 0x35, 0x36, 0x37`. x86-64 is little-endian, so a 64-bit read treats the *lowest* address as the *least-significant* byte — the byte order for the integer is the reverse of the address order:
$$\text{canary} = \mathtt{0x37363534\,33323130}$$
(most-significant byte `0x37`, from the highest address, down to least-significant byte `0x30`, from the lowest). This was checked both with Python (`struct.unpack("<Q", bytes.fromhex("3031323334353637"))`) and by compiling and running the equivalent C snippet on this machine; both give `0x3736353433323130`, which of course still mismatches the original canary and would still trigger `__stack_chk_fail`.

The general lesson carries directly into constructing an exploit string: any multi-byte value placed on the stack — a canary, a return address, a gadget pointer in a ROP chain — must be written **least-significant byte first**. Writing the bytes of an address in the "obvious" left-to-right order silently reverses it, and the exploit jumps to the wrong place entirely.

pitfalls: Assuming NX alone stops exploitation — code injection is defeated, but ROP never fetches from the stack, so NX gives it nothing to block.
Assuming ASLR alone is sufficient — a single leaked pointer (uninitialized read, format-string bug, or brute force on a small address space) collapses it to one guess.

Believing a stack canary catches every corruption — it only detects overwrites that pass through the checked word on the way to the return address; a hijacked function pointer used before return, or a heap overflow, bypasses it entirely.

Forgetting that -fstack-protector is heuristic, not universal — GCC's default flag only instruments functions it judges to have a vulnerable local (roughly, an array of at least 8 bytes); a smaller or differently-typed buffer can be skipped.

Writing an exploit's embedded address in the wrong byte order — x86-64 is little-endian, so a multi-byte value must be written least-significant-byte first, exactly like the canary bytes in this card's worked example.
Treating a heap overflow like a stack overflow — heap corruption targets allocator metadata or adjacent objects, not a return address, so canaries and NX don't apply the same way.
applications: GCC/glibc: -fstack-protector-strong is the default canary heuristic on most mainstream Linux distributions.
Linux, Windows and macOS kernels ship NX (the page-table XD bit) and ASLR (randomized mmap/stack/PIE base addresses) enabled by default.
Apple Silicon's arm64e adds hardware pointer authentication (PAC), cryptographically signing return addresses and function pointers as a hardware-level answer to ROP/JOP chains.

Browsers and OS kernels deploy Control Flow Guard / Clang CFI to restrict indirect-branch targets after a memory-corruption bug, closing off ROP even when other mitigations have already been defeated.
CS:APP's Attack Lab (CTARGET/RTARGET) is the pedagogical environment CENG331 uses to practice exactly the code-injection and ROP primitives described in this card.
exam_focus: METU's 2025 midterm (Q14) tested this as a multi-select, negatively-marked question: the correct mitigations against stack code injection were stack canaries, a non-executable stack, and stack address randomization; 'digitally signing the executable on disk' was the deliberate wrong option, since it guards against static tampering, not a runtime overflow.

CENG331's Attack Lab (Homework 2) is graded phase by phase: 10/25/25 points for code-injection phases against touch1/touch2/touch3 on CTARGET, and 35 points for a return-oriented-programming phase against touch2 on RTARGET, with 50 of the available points required for the homework to count toward the course grade.

self_check.question: RTARGET combines ASLR and a non-executable stack. Why does return-oriented programming defeat both at once, and what single additional mitigation (mentioned in this card) would close that remaining gap?
self_check.answer: Code injection needs two things: a way to execute attacker-supplied bytes, and a predictable address to jump to. NX removes the first by making the stack non-executable, and ASLR removes the second by making the stack address unpredictable. ROP sidesteps both at once by never introducing new bytes to execute — it only reuses instruction sequences (gadgets) already sitting in the executable, already-mapped code segment, so NX is irrelevant, and it chains them through return addresses placed on the still-writable stack, so a non-executable stack doesn't stop it either. What ROP still needs is a predictable address for each gadget in the *code* segment. PIE (position-independent executables) closes exactly that gap, randomizing the code segment's base address the same way ASLR randomizes the stack, so gadget addresses become unpredictable too.

self_check.question: A frame is `struct frame { char buf[8]; uint64_t canary; }`, canary initialized to `0xDEADBEEFCAFEBABE`. An unbounded copy writes the 16 ASCII bytes `CAFEBABE01234567` (no null terminator) into `buf`. What does the canary check see, and does the function abort?
self_check.answer: The first 8 bytes, `CAFEBABE`, fill `buf[0..7]` completely. The next 8 bytes, `01234567` (ASCII `0x30..0x37`), land exactly on the canary's 8 bytes, in address order `0x30,0x31,0x32,0x33,0x34,0x35,0x36,0x37`. x86-64 is little-endian, so the 64-bit value read back reverses that address order: most-significant byte from the highest address (`0x37`) down to least-significant byte from the lowest (`0x30`), giving `0x3736353433323130`. Checked in Python: `struct.unpack('<Q', bytes.fromhex('3031323334353637'))` returns exactly `0x3736353433323130`. Since `0x3736353433323130 ≠ 0xDEADBEEFCAFEBABE`, the comparison fails and the function reports stack smashing and aborts instead of returning — it does not matter that the overwrite used printable ASCII rather than 'random-looking' bytes; any value that isn't the original canary is caught.

self_check.question: A server is compiled with -fstack-protector-all (canaries on every function) and runs under default ASLR, but its stack is intentionally executable to support a JIT feature. Given only a classic sequential stack buffer overflow and no separate information leak, which of this card's three basic defenses actually stops an exploit here, and how would the answer change if the attacker could also read arbitrary stack memory before triggering the overflow?
self_check.answer: With only a sequential overflow and no leak, the canary is what stops it: any overwrite reaching the return address must first overwrite the canary sitting between it and the buffer, and -fstack-protector-all guarantees every function checks that canary before returning, so the corrupted return address is caught and the process aborts rather than jumping anywhere. NX contributes nothing here, since the stack is deliberately executable by design; ASLR only raises the cost of guessing an address correctly, it doesn't detect or prevent the overwrite itself. If the attacker can also read arbitrary stack memory first, the calculus changes: they can read the canary's actual current value at its known offset and echo it back unchanged in the overflow payload, so the canary check passes even though the return address right after it is still overwritten with attacker data pointing into the executable stack. A single arbitrary-read primitive turns a fully mitigated-looking configuration back into a working code-injection exploit — which is why canaries are described as raising the cost of an attack, not making overflow bugs harmless.

key_points: An unchecked write into a stack buffer can overwrite the return address stored in the same frame.
Canaries detect a corrupted path to the return address before ret executes; they don't catch every corruption.
ASLR randomizes addresses so an injected-code pointer usually fails; one pointer leak defeats it.
NX/DEP marks the stack non-executable, defeating code injection but not code-reuse attacks (ROP).
ROP chains gadgets — byte sequences ending in 0xc3 — via repeated ret; it needs no injected code.
x86-64 is little-endian: a multi-byte value written onto the stack must be written least-significant byte first.
tagline: A stack overflow can overwrite a return address; canaries, ASLR and NX/DEP each close a different path back to control of %rip.
tldr: An unchecked write into a stack buffer can overwrite the return address stored in the same frame, letting an attacker redirect control flow by **code injection** — writing shellcode into the buffer and pointing the return address at it. **Stack canaries**, **ASLR** and **NX/DEP** each block one part of that primitive, but **return-oriented programming** defeats all three at once by chaining existing, executable code fragments (**gadgets**) through repeated `ret` instructions instead of injecting anything new. CS:APP's Attack Lab (`CTARGET`/`RTARGET`) is built to practice exactly these two attack classes.
